about: How a satellite works, part by part, through one real Indian satellite — NISAR, the NASA–ISRO radar launched from Sriharikota in July 2025 — and where India stands in space: the fleet, the launches, the money, the dependence and the next steps.

nisar.massNote: ISRO gives about 2,400 kg lift-off mass.

firstLight.what: First-day payload operations of the S-band SAR

split.india: The spacecraft bus, the S-band radar, the launch vehicle and launch services
split.us: The L-band radar, the solid-state recorder, GPS and the 3.5 Gbps Ka-band telecom system; the radar structure was integrated and tested at JPL, then delivered to ISRO

parts.name: 12 m reflector
parts.does: A gold-plated wire-mesh dish that folds like an umbrella for launch and opens in orbit. It catches the radar echo from the ground and focuses it on the feeds.
parts.inNisar: 12 m across, shared by both radars; fully deployed on 15 August 2025.

parts.name: 9 m deployable boom
parts.does: A hinged arm that unfolds in stages to hold the reflector far enough from the spacecraft for the radar beam to form.

parts.name: L-band radar (24 cm)
parts.does: Sends pulses that pass through leaves and dry soil, so it sees forest structure and ground that moves by centimetres.
parts.inNisar: Built by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

parts.name: S-band radar (~10 cm)
parts.does: A shorter wavelength, more sensitive to crops, snow and surface roughness. Together with L-band it reads two layers of the same ground.
parts.inNisar: Built by ISRO; first-day operations began on 19 August 2025.

parts.name: Radar instrument structure
parts.does: The frame that carries both radars' feeds and electronics and anchors the boom.
parts.inNisar: Integrated and tested at JPL with both radars, then delivered to ISRO to be joined to the bus.

parts.name: Solid-state recorder
parts.does: Stores radar data until the satellite passes over a ground station.
parts.inNisar: About 9 terabits at end of life.

parts.name: Ka-band data downlink
parts.does: A high-frequency radio that sends the stored data to ground stations in minutes-long passes.

parts.name: GPS receivers
parts.does: Fix the satellite's position precisely, so each radar image can be placed on the map and compared with the last.

parts.name: Spacecraft bus
parts.does: The body that keeps everything alive: structure, power, pointing, propulsion, heat and the radio link for commands.

parts.name: Solar array
parts.does: Panels of solar cells turned towards the Sun, generating the satellite's power whenever it is in daylight.
parts.inNisar: Two motorised arrays, part of ISRO’s bus; about 5 kW in full sun. The cell supplier is not published.

stat.label: from two arrays, about 23 m², in full sun

parts.name: Battery
parts.does: Stores daylight power for the minutes of each orbit spent in Earth's shadow, and for radar bursts larger than the array alone supplies.

parts.name: Reaction wheels
parts.does: Flywheels spun faster or slower by motors; as one speeds up, the satellite turns the other way. This is how it points without spending fuel.

parts.name: Star sensors
parts.does: Small cameras that photograph the stars and match them to a catalogue, telling the computer exactly which way the satellite faces.

parts.name: Propellant tank and thrusters
parts.does: Small rocket motors that raise the orbit after launch, hold it against drag and, at the end of life, lower it.

parts.name: Thermal blankets and radiators
parts.does: Multi-layer insulation keeps heat in on the cold side; mirrored radiators throw it away on the hot side, holding electronics near room temperature.

parts.name: Command and telemetry antennas
parts.does: Low-rate radios for the satellite's health reports and the commands that run it, heard by ISRO's tracking network.
parts.inNisar: Part of ISRO's bus; tracked by ISTRAC.

dependence.what: ISRO's own figures for imported content — mainly electronics and packages in satellites
dependence.progress: ISRO and the government's Semiconductor Laboratory have developed four indigenous integrated circuits for launch-vehicle avionics.

fleet.note: Operational satellites per a Parliament reply. A catalogue count of Indian objects in orbit, including dead ones, is about 117, with 70 active by KeepTrack's count.
fleet.plan: ISRO's chairman said in December 2025 the fleet should grow to nearly 150 within two to three years.

places.name: Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota
places.note: India's spaceport; every orbital launch since 1979, including NISAR and Vikram-1.

places.name: Kulasekarapattinam (under construction)
places.note: India's second spaceport, for small rockets; commissioning targeted in 2026–27, ₹985.96 crore allocated.

timeline.what: Chandrayaan-3 lands near the Moon's south pole — the first landing there.
Aditya-L1 reaches the Sun–Earth L1 point to watch the solar corona.
SpaDeX docks two satellites in orbit — India the fourth country to do it, after the US, Russia and China.
ISRO's 100th launch from Sriharikota: GSLV-F15 with navigation satellite NVS-02.
PSLV-C61 fails in its third stage; EOS-09 lost.
Shubhanshu Shukla flies to the ISS on Axiom-4 — 18 days aboard.
GSLV-F16 launches NISAR, the NASA–ISRO radar satellite.
LVM3 launches BlueBird 6, about 6,100 kg — the heaviest satellite launched from India, for a US customer.
PSLV-C62 fails near the end of its third stage — the second PSLV loss in eight months, and the first foreign customer payloads ISRO has lost.
Skyroot's Vikram-1 reaches orbit — India's first private orbital rocket.
Gaganyaan G1, the uncrewed test of India’s crew capsule with the robot Vyommitra aboard, planned for the last quarter of 2026 — after a December 2025 target slipped.

unspent.text: Since 2020 the department has not spent even its revised budgets, leaving more than ₹12,000 crore unused, by one analysis.
